integrations.title: What it reads, where it lands
integrations.lead: No testimonials, no avatar wall, no user count. Every card below either ships a connector in this release or says plainly that it does not have one yet, so the wall itself is a status report.
integrations.plannedLine: Planned connector. Meter it today through manual entry or ingest.

claude.detail: Parses the rate limit block Claude Code already hands to your statusline command. It asks nothing of Anthropic on its own.

openRouter.detail: Parses the credits shape OpenRouter documents. The key belongs in your operating system credential store, never in a file.

codex.detail: Parses the usage shape the Codex tooling produces. The shape is internal, so it can change without notice, and it fails closed when it does.

antigravity.detail: Parses the quota shape the Antigravity tooling produces. Internal too, marked as such, and never repaired or rewritten.

openCode.tag: reads a session you already opened
openCode.detail: Describes the usage view behind an existing session. It carries the highest automation risk of the six and stops the moment that session expires.

manualEntry.name: Manual entry
manualEntry.detail: Budgets you maintain by hand, for a self hosted model or any subscription without a connector. It never breaks and never guesses.

statusline.name: Claude Code statusline
statusline.detail: One line beside your prompt: the worst meter per provider with a reason code in front. It falls back to the cache and never blocks the tool that called it.

promptHook.name: Claude Code prompt hook
promptHook.detail: A bounded block on prompt submit, fenced in an explicit untrusted data boundary. When every provider is unknown it injects nothing at all.

shell.name: Any shell
shell.detail: The whole snapshot as a table for you or as JSON for a script. No network call, no account, no daemon in the middle.

fileWriter.name: Any tool that can write a file
fileWriter.detail: One generic command takes a payload for any connector, so a provider without an integration can still be fed from a script you control.

ci.name: Continuous integration
ci.detail: Export the cache as JSON and assert on it in a pipeline. Every release is tested on Windows and Linux on every push.

ownFrontend.name: Your own front end
ownFrontend.detail: The cache is a plain document on your disk with a versioned schema. Read it and build whatever view you want.

worksWith.title: Works with your tools
worksWith.lead: One meter over every subscription you already hold. Each connector reads a shape that something on your machine already wrote, and in this release not one of them touches the network.

today.label: Ships today
today.note: Six connectors ship in this release

planned.label: Planned
planned.note: Known, named, and not written yet

worksWith.footnote: Every connector ships marked UNVERIFIED, the honest default: no verifier has confirmed a shape against a live account yet. Three read interfaces internal to somebody else's tooling, and when one changes, that provider fails closed to unknown rather than guessing. Every connector and its real state.
worksWith.manualNote: Every tool on this page can be metered today. Write the numbers down with manual entry, or pipe a payload in with ingest from any script you control, and it lands in the same snapshot as a connector.

runsWhere.title: Runs where you work
runsWhere.lead: Windows, macOS and Linux, from a terminal, a statusline, a prompt hook or a script, and in any browser through the web app. One local cache, read by whatever you point at it.
runsWhere.screenshotsNote: Screenshots of the web app at phone size, against the project's synthetic fixtures, declared here in words rather than stamped over the pictures. The same reading opens in the <webApp>web app</webApp> and installs to a home screen. Native mobile applications are planned and not built.

webApp.title: Web app
webApp.lead: A browser is the one surface every device already has. This one runs the same engine as the command line tool, on a document you give it, parsed entirely in the tab, with nothing uploaded, no account anywhere, and nothing to install before it works.

sameEngine.title: The same engine, in the tab
sameEngine.detail: Not a second implementation. The core, the connectors and the adapter are mirrored from the command line tool into the browser bundle, so a reading here and a reading in a terminal cannot disagree.

handDocument.title: You hand it the document
handDocument.detail: Paste or drop what openlimiter export prints. A browser tab cannot read your disk by itself, and nothing is uploaded to make up for that: parsing happens in the tab and no request leaves it.

offline.title: Installs, and works offline
offline.detail: Add it to a phone or desktop home screen and it opens like an application. A service worker keeps it working with no network at all, because it never needed one.

scriptable.title: Fully scriptable
scriptable.lead: Everything the tool knows, it will print. A table for you, one line for a statusline, a bounded block for an agent, or plain JSON for anything else.
scriptable.note: Every block above is verbatim standard output, captured against the project's synthetic fixtures. Add export for the same state as JSON, and doctor when a connector stops parsing.

agentContext.title: Read, bound, hand over
agentContext.lead: A block injected into a prompt is an injection surface. This one carries enum codes, bounded numbers and timestamps, and it says so about itself in its own opening tag.

providerTextNeverCrosses.title: Provider text never crosses
providerTextNeverCrosses.detail: Parsers keep known numbers and known timestamps. Labels, messages, account text, markup and unknown fields are discarded before anything reaches policy code, so no provider's prose can become an instruction to your agent.

enumCodesOnly.title: Enum codes only
enumCodesOnly.detail: The advice engine emits provider codes, reason codes, bounded percentages, freshness codes and timestamps. The adapter validates every one of them again on the way out.

silenceBeatsGuess.title: Silence beats a guess
silenceBeatsGuess.detail: If every provider is unknown, the hook injects nothing at all. It reads the local cache, makes no network request, and exits 0 whatever happens.

adviceNotRouting.title: Advice, not routing
adviceNotRouting.detail: OpenLimiter tells your agent what is left and what that suggests. It does not switch providers for you, does not bypass a limit, and does not touch how anything authenticates. The decision stays yours.

whatLeaves.question: What actually leaves my machine?
whatLeaves.answer: Nothing. There is no telemetry, no analytics, and no OpenLimiter server to receive anything. This release performs no provider egress at all: every connector is a parser over data that something else already wrote to your disk or piped to standard input.

safeToPoint.question: Is it safe to point at my tools?
safeToPoint.answer: OpenLimiter opens what your installed tools already store, read only, and never rewrites, repairs or migrates them. Every parser keeps bounded numbers and timestamps and discards provider text before anything reaches your agent.

promptHook.question: Can the prompt hook break my session?
promptHook.answer: No. The hook reads the local cache, makes no network request, injects nothing when every provider is unknown, and exits 0 whatever happens. The statusline behaves the same way: if input is absent or malformed it falls back to the cache and reports unknown.

providersToday.question: Which providers work today?
providersToday.answer: Six connectors ship: Claude through the native statusline payload, OpenRouter through its documented shape, Codex and Antigravity through internal shapes that may break, OpenCode through an existing session that may break, and manual entry. Every one is marked UNVERIFIED until an explicit verifier exists.

apiKey.question: Do I need an API key?
apiKey.answer: Not to start. The Claude path reads a payload Claude Code already hands your statusline, and the manual path needs nothing at all. OpenRouter is the one connector that expects a key of your own, and that key belongs in your operating system credential store.

routing.question: Does it route my requests for me?
routing.answer: No, and it is not going to. OpenLimiter provides advice. It does not route requests automatically, does not bypass a limit, and does not touch how your agent authenticates. The decision stays with you.

connectorBreaks.question: What happens when a connector breaks?
connectorBreaks.answer: Unofficial shapes change without notice. When one does, parsing fails closed: that provider returns to unknown, the other providers are unaffected, and nothing invents a number to fill the gap. Unknown never becomes zero.

desktopOrPhone.question: Is there a desktop or phone app?
desktopOrPhone.answer: The desktop tray application is built and packaged for Windows, macOS and Linux, and every build is attached to the release on GitHub. None of them are code signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper warn the first time you open one, and the download page says how to get past that. On a phone, the web app opens in the browser and installs to a home screen. Native iOS and Android applications are not built, nothing is in a store, and there is no waiting list. The download page lists every platform with its real state.

free.question: Is it free?
free.answer: Everything that runs locally is free and always will be, under Apache 2.0: every connector, the agent context block, themes, the whole command line tool, and all three ingestion paths, with no usage limit and no account. Desktop notifications are not built yet and will be free too.

pro.question: What is OpenLimiter Pro?
pro.answer: A planned paid tier at $5 a month, founding price, for the things that can only run on servers: encrypted synchronisation across your devices, push notifications to your phone, a smart limiter that routes between your models from live budget state, email alerts and a weekly digest, delivery rules, hosted history and burn trends, priority connector requests, and a team tier later. It is not built. There is no checkout and no waiting list, and nothing that runs locally today ever moves behind it.

pricing.title: Pricing
pricing.lead: Everything that runs on your machine is free, and that is not a launch offer. The only thing that could ever cost money is a service running on servers, because servers cost money to run.

free.lead: The whole local product, for everybody, with no account anywhere in it.
free.footnote: Open source under <licence>Apache 2.0</licence>, so this cannot be taken away later. The licence is the promise.

about.lead: OpenLimiter is an independent open source project for people who hold several AI coding subscriptions at once and would rather know which one still has room than find out the hard way, mid task.
about.description: It is built around three commitments that are easy to state and awkward to keep. If it saves you an afternoon, sponsorship is the best way to keep the connectors working as the shapes underneath them shift. Reporting a connector that broke is worth just as much.

runsLocal.title: It runs on your machine
runsLocal.detail: Every connector in this release is a parser over something already on your disk. No provider egress, no daemon, no account.

reportsNobody.title: It reports to nobody
reportsNobody.detail: The software has no telemetry, no analytics, and no OpenLimiter server for anything to reach. This website keeps cookieless page counts only, with no cookies and nothing personal.

unknownStaysUnknown.title: Unknown stays unknown
unknownStaysUnknown.detail: A missing number never becomes a confident one. When a shape changes underneath a connector, that provider fails closed.

linux.name: Linux

linux.requirement: Node 24 or newer and pnpm 9.15.0, which the repository pins.

web-app.name: Web app
web-app.summary: Nothing to install. The web app runs the same engine as the command line tool inside the browser tab, on a document you paste or drop, and it installs to a phone or desktop home screen and keeps working offline. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account.

desktop.name: Desktop application
desktop.summary: A tray icon beside the system clock, reading the same local cache the command line tool writes, so quota is glanceable with no terminal open. It is packaged for Windows, macOS and Linux, and every build is attached to the same release. There is no automatic update channel yet, so a new version means downloading it again.
desktop.note: None of the desktop builds are code signed yet. Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper both warn on first run, and each platform row above says how to get past it.

index.title: Getting started
index.metaTitle: Getting started: install and meter your quota
index.description: Install the workspace, run the demo, and wire OpenLimiter into Claude Code in a few minutes.
index.lead: OpenLimiter is a quota meter for the AI subscriptions you already pay for. It runs on your machine, reads what your tools already wrote there, and hands your coding agents a bounded picture of what budget is left.

what-you-need.title: What you need
what-you-need.local: Everything runs locally. No account is created, no key is required to start, and no request leaves your machine during any of the steps below.

install.title: Install OpenLimiter
install.intro: Install the command line tool globally, then run its synthetic demo.
install.demo: openlimiter demo renders synthetic fixtures. It proves the binary works without touching any real account, and every number it prints is invented.

first-data.title: Give it something to meter
first-data.parser: OpenLimiter never contacts a provider in this release. It parses data that something else already put in front of it. Until one of the ingestion paths runs, every command honestly reports unknown.
first-data.statusline: The path that needs no extra work is the Claude Code statusline. Claude Code runs your statusline command on every render and writes a JSON object describing the current session to that command's standard input. When that object carries a rate limit block, OpenLimiter validates it, caches it, and renders the fresh numbers in the same call.
first-data.fallback: Not every Claude Code version sends rate limit fields. If yours does not, this path stays quiet and the two manual paths still work. The <docs>ingestion page</docs> covers all three.

claude-code.title: Wire Claude Code
claude-code.intro: Add this to your Claude Code settings.json. The global install makes the openlimiter command available to Claude Code.
claude-code.calloutTitle: The hook cannot break your session
claude-code.calloutBody: The statusline is the only path that writes. The hook reads the cache, makes no network request of any kind, injects nothing when every provider is unknown, and exits 0 whatever happens.

from-source.title: Contribute from source
from-source.intro: Use the repository toolchain when you want to contribute.
from-source.buildOrder: The build has to run before the type check, because each package resolves its neighbours through the declaration files the build produces.

why-openlimiter.title: Why OpenLimiter
why-openlimiter.description: When you hold several AI coding subscriptions the scarce resource stops being money and becomes quota.
why-openlimiter.lead: When you hold several AI coding subscriptions, the scarce resource stops being money and becomes quota. You already paid. The question that decides your afternoon is which of those plans still has room left.

the-problem.title: The problem
the-problem.interruption: A developer running two or three coding agents ends the week with the same recurring interruption. One plan hits its window, the agent stops mid task, and the work pauses while a human goes hunting through dashboards to find out which other subscription is still usable.
the-problem.scattered: The information exists. It is scattered across a statusline payload, a local usage file, a billing page, and a credit balance, in four different shapes, none of which the agent can see.

what-it-does.title: What OpenLimiter does about it
what-it-does.intro: OpenLimiter reads quota for supported AI subscriptions on your own machine, normalises every reading into one schema, and feeds bounded budget state plus routing advice into the coding agents' own context. The first adapter is a Claude Code statusline and prompt hook.

bullets.read: Read. Connectors parse shapes that a provider or a local tool already produced. They perform no network access in this release.
bullets.normalise: Normalise. One snapshot schema with closed enums, bounded percentages, and derived freshness. Unknown stays unknown and never becomes a fabricated zero.
bullets.advise: Advise. A compact statusline for you, and a bounded context block for your agent that carries enum codes, numbers, and timestamps only.

what-it-is-not.title: What it deliberately is not
what-it-is-not.calloutBody: OpenLimiter provides routing advice. It does not route requests for you, it does not bypass a limit, and it never mutates a provider's authentication artifacts. The decision stays with you and your agent.

bullets.proxy: It is not a proxy. Your requests keep going straight to your provider.
bullets.dashboard: It is not a dashboard service. There is no OpenLimiter server, no account, and no telemetry.
bullets.billing: It is not a billing tool. It reports how much of a window you have consumed, not what you will be charged.

unknown-stays-unknown.title: Unknown stays unknown
unknown-stays-unknown.body: Missing, expired, malformed, and unrecognised input all resolve to unknown. A connector that cannot read something says so. Nothing in the codebase turns an absent reading into a zero, because a fake zero would make an agent behave as though a plan were exhausted.

truncated-not-rounded.title: Percentages are truncated, never rounded up
truncated-not-rounded.body: A meter at 99.99% renders as 99.9%. A cap is only ever claimed once it has actually been reached.

one-bad-row.title: One bad row does not lose a provider
one-bad-row.body: A row that fails validation is dropped and the remaining rows still count. One expired window is not a reason to forget a whole subscription.

local-first.title: Local first, with no server to trust
local-first.body: Everything is written to a local state directory under your own user account. See configuration for where that is, and security and privacy for what that buys you. The licence is Apache 2.0 and the whole thing is UNVERIFIED by its own labels until a verifier exists.

providers.description: The six connectors that ship today, what each one reads, and how likely it is to break.
providers.lead: Six connectors ship today. Each one carries its own honest labels describing where its credentials come from, how official its data interface is, and how likely it is to break.

the-six.calloutBody: UNVERIFIED is the honest default. It means no explicit verifier has confirmed the shape against a live account, so openlimiter doctor reports drift as unverified rather than claiming a connector is known good.

how-data-arrives.title: How data actually arrives
how-data-arrives.intro: This is the part that surprises people, so it is worth stating plainly. In this release no connector performs network access. Every one of them is a parser, and something else has to hand it a document.

bullets.claude: claude is fed by the statusline payload arriving on standard input. That path is automatic once Claude Code is wired up.
bullets.manual: manual is fed by a document you place in the state directory.
bullets.ingestOnly: codex, antigravity, opencode and openrouter have no local reader yet. They accept data through openlimiter ingest --provider '' and nothing else.

how-data-arrives.exactShapes: The <docs>ingestion page</docs> documents all three paths and the exact shapes they accept.

labels.title: Reading the labels
labels.intro: Every snapshot carries four labels, so a surface can always tell a reader how much to trust a number.
labels.caption: The four connector labels and their meaning

drift.title: What drift looks like
drift.body: Unofficial interfaces change without notice. When a shape moves, parsing fails closed: the affected provider returns to unknown, the other providers are unaffected, and nothing invents a number to fill the gap.

openrouter-key.title: The OpenRouter credential
openrouter-key.intro: OpenRouter is the one connector that expects a key of your own. That key belongs in your operating system credential store and nowhere else. It must never appear in repository files, cache files, exports, diagnostics, fixtures, or logs.
openrouter-key.calloutBody: The credential library adapter is deliberately stubbed, so openlimiter init cannot store a key until you supply a driver. Until then, feed OpenRouter through the ingest command like any other provider.

not-yet.title: Connectors that do not exist yet
not-yet.body: Only the six above are real. Anything else you might hope for is not built, is not scheduled, and should not be assumed. If a subscription has no connector, the manual path covers it today with numbers you enter yourself.

connections.title: Connections
connections.metaTitle: Connections: source chips and the state vocabulary
connections.description: What each connection state and source chip actually means, stated honestly, including what Import only does and does not do.
connections.lead: Every provider shows two things: a chip naming where its numbers came from, and, underneath, a state drawn from one vocabulary the whole product shares. This page names every state in it, says plainly what Import only means, and says what changes once a live connection exists.

chips.title: The chip on a provider today
chips.intro: A parser existing is not a connection, so no card in the dashboard is ever labelled connected on the strength of one. Every provider instead carries a chip naming how its numbers actually reached this device. There are three, today.
chips.caption: The three source chips shown in the dashboard today

localCli.meaning: A tool on this machine writes the payload, and OpenLimiter reads what it wrote.

importOnly.meaning: The payload shape is parsed. Nothing here signs in or fetches it, so you supply the document.

manual.meaning: Figures you keep yourself. Nothing is read from an account.

chips.calloutBody: A parser exists for that provider's document, and OpenLimiter understands the shape when it sees one. Nothing here signs in, holds a key, or fetches anything on its own. A reading arrives only once you hand OpenLimiter that document yourself, by pasting it or by running openlimiter ingest --provider ''. See ingestion for the exact paths.

vocabulary.title: The full connection vocabulary
vocabulary.intro: Underneath the three chips sits a larger vocabulary: thirteen named states, one module in the core package the whole product is built from, each with one plain sentence rather than a log line. It exists so a connection's state is a value every surface reads the same way, never a sentence each one is free to invent for itself.
vocabulary.caption: Every state in the connection vocabulary, and what each one means

detected.meaning: Found on this machine but not collecting yet.

degraded.meaning: The provider is refusing reads for now.

stale.meaning: The last reading is older than it should be.

importOnly.meaning: Reads only what you import. Nothing is collected automatically.

manual.meaning: Shows the plan you entered yourself.

unsupported.meaning: No safe automatic source exists for this product yet.

error.meaning: This connection failed and needs a look.

bullets.declared: IMPORT_ONLY, MANUAL and UNSUPPORTED are declared rather than attempted, by design: the product states them outright, and nothing that happens afterward, a response, a failure, a timeout, is allowed to quietly promote one of them to CONNECTED. Only OpenLimiter itself declaring otherwise moves a connection out of one.
bullets.lifecycle: The rest name a lifecycle a live reader would move a connection through: found but not yet collecting, waiting on a credential, connecting, connected, and, when something goes wrong, degraded, stale, expired, or needing a look.

what-this-is-not-claiming.title: What this page is not claiming
what-this-is-not-claiming.body: Not that all thirteen are on screen. What the dashboard actually renders today is the simpler, three chip vocabulary above, built for a release where nothing performs a network read. The thirteen states are real and tested in the core package this product is built from, and they name the general lifecycle any connection follows once a live reader exists. No surface renders those words yet, because nothing today does the thing that would put a connection into one of them: no reader, no request, nothing to fail, expire, or need a credential for.

what-changes.title: What changes when a live connection ships
what-changes.intro: Nothing on this page is a date or a promise. When a provider gains a real reader, the honest description of it stops being a fixed chip and starts being whichever of the thirteen states above actually fits at that moment: detected, waiting on a credential, connecting, connected, or, when something goes wrong, degraded, stale, or needing a look. That is the reason to name the whole vocabulary now, before any of it is reachable, so the sentence a person reads does not change on the day the state underneath it starts moving.
what-changes.noReader: No provider has that reader today. See the <roadmap>roadmap</roadmap> for what is planned and what is not, and <providers>supported providers</providers> for what each connector can actually do right now.

ingestion.title: Ingestion
ingestion.description: The three offline paths that put quota data in front of OpenLimiter, and what each one expects.
ingestion.lead: Three paths put quota data in front of OpenLimiter. All three are offline. None of them reaches the network, and until one of them runs, every command honestly reports unknown.

statusline.title: 1. The Claude Code statusline payload
statusline.intro: This is the path that needs no extra work once Claude Code is wired up. Claude Code runs your statusline command on every render and writes a JSON object describing the current session to that command's standard input. When that object carries a rate limit block, openlimiter statusline validates it, writes it to the cache, and renders the fresh numbers in the same call.
statusline.blockLabel: the block it reads, from Anthropic's own statusline documentation
statusline.fields: used_percentage is the share of the window already used, from 0 to 100. resets_at is a Unix epoch number in seconds, not a date string. Both field names and the epoch encoding come from Anthropic's published statusline documentation rather than from this project, and each window is independently optional: a payload naming only one of them is one complete meter, not a partial one.

bullets.rateLimits: rate_limits appears only for Claude.ai subscribers on a Pro or Max plan, and only after the first API response of a session. A payload with no rate_limits block is the ordinary shape of a free account or a session that has not called the API yet, not an error.
bullets.implausibleReset: A reset implausibly far out for its own window, a five hour window resetting days away, is dropped on its own rather than trusted. The other window still counts.

statusline.ignored: Anything else in the session object is ignored. A window that fails validation is dropped and the other window still counts.
statusline.calloutTitle: This path can never break your statusline
statusline.calloutBody: If standard input is absent, empty, malformed, or carries no recognisable rate limit field, the statusline falls back to the cache and reports unknown. It never blocks and never fails. Not every Claude Code version sends rate limit fields; if yours does not, this path simply stays quiet.

manual-document.title: 2. A manual document on disk
manual-document.intro: Write manual.json inside the state directory and every command picks it up. See configuration for where that directory lives on each platform.

manual-rules.title: The rules each row must satisfy

bullets.name: name is one uppercase identifier of up to 32 characters, starting with a letter.
bullets.resetAt: reset_at is an ISO instant in the future.
bullets.ten: Up to ten meters are read. Rows past the tenth are ignored.
bullets.dropped: A row that breaks any of those rules is dropped, and the remaining rows still count. Nothing is repaired.

manual-document.refresh: Run openlimiter snapshot --refresh to fold the file into the cache.

ingest-command.title: 3. The generic ingest command
ingest-command.intro: Any script or agent can hand OpenLimiter a document without a provider integration. The command reads standard input, or an inline document passed with --payload.
ingest-command.provider: Without a provider flag the document is treated as a manual document, so the resulting snapshot is labelled with manual precision. With --provider '' the document is handed to that connector's own parser and keeps that connector's labels.
ingest-command.validIds: Valid provider ids are claude, openrouter, codex, antigravity, opencode, and manual. An unknown id is a usage error and exits 2.

merging.title: What happens to the data
merging.intro: Ingested rows merge into one cache under the same lock every other writer uses, so nothing already cached is lost and two writers observing different providers cannot silently drop each other's rows.

bullets.validated: Values are validated against the snapshot schema before anything is written.
bullets.bounds: Percentages stay between 0 and 100. A value outside that range is not clamped, it is dropped.
bullets.atomic: Every write lands through an atomic replacement, so a reader observes either the previous content or the new content and never a partial file.
bullets.freshness: Freshness is derived from when a reading was observed and when it expires, so stale data is labelled rather than silently reused as current.

merging.nothingSurvives: Nothing survives validation? The command reports that no bounded meter survived and exits with a failure, rather than writing a placeholder.

agent-context.title: Agent context
agent-context.description: What the Claude Code statusline and prompt hook inject, and the boundary that keeps provider text out.
agent-context.lead: Two surfaces reach your agent: a one line statusline for you to read, and a bounded context block for the model. This page documents exactly what each one contains and the boundary that keeps provider text out of both.

statusline.title: The statusline
statusline.intro: One line, rendered on every Claude Code statusline call. It names the worst state across your providers, lists the providers with a usable reading, and names the ones that are unknown.
statusline.truncation: Usage is truncated, never rounded upward, so a meter at 99.99% reads as 99.9%. When nothing usable is cached the whole line reduces to OpenLimiter UNKNOWN.

context-block.title: The context block
context-block.intro: The prompt hook emits a small block on UserPromptSubmit. It is plain text with one field per line, wrapped in an explicit untrusted data boundary.

fields.title: Every field it can contain
fields.caption: Fields in the agent context block

recommendationCode.meaning: PREFER when a provider is worth routing to, or NONE when nothing usable stands out.

recommendationProvider.meaning: The provider code the advice points at. Present only when the code is PREFER.

recommendationReason.meaning: Why that provider: LOWEST_USAGE today. An enum, never prose.

notice.meaning: A fixed sentence telling the model to treat the block as untrusted data.

reason.meaning: The worst state across providers: HEALTHY, NEAR_CAP at 80% or above, or AT_CAP at 100%.

provider.meaning: One line per provider with a usable reading, carrying state of fresh or stale, a bounded usage_percent, and a reset_at instant or NONE.

unknown.meaning: The providers with no usable reading, or NONE when every provider was read.

boundary.title: The safety boundary
boundary.calloutTitle: Provider text never reaches your agent
boundary.calloutBody: Provider responses are untrusted data. Connector parsers select known numeric fields and known timestamps, then discard labels, messages, account text, markup, and every unknown field. The advice engine emits only provider enum codes, reason enum codes, bounded percentages, freshness enum codes, and timestamps. The Claude Code adapter validates all of those again before writing the block.
boundary.injectionSurface: This matters because a block injected into a prompt is an injection surface. If a provider could put arbitrary text into your agent's context through a billing message or an account name, that text would arrive with the authority of your own tooling. Nothing in this pipeline can carry it.

bullets.unknown: If every provider is unknown, the adapter injects nothing at all.
bullets.validation: If the advice fails its own validation, the adapter injects nothing.
bullets.cache: If the cache cannot be read, the hook returns an empty result rather than guessing.

hook-behaviour.title: How the hook behaves

bullets.readsOnly: It reads the cache only. It performs no network request of any kind and writes nothing.
bullets.exitsZero: It exits 0 whatever happens, including on internal failure, so it cannot break a session.
bullets.inspect: Running openlimiter hook in a terminal prints exactly what would be injected, which is a safe way to inspect it before wiring it into a real session.

hook-behaviour.writes: The statusline is the only path that writes. See <config>configuration</config> for the exact Claude Code settings, and <cli>the CLI reference</cli> for the commands.

configuration.title: Configuration
configuration.description: The state directory, the configuration file, the cache, and the settings Claude Code needs.
configuration.lead: OpenLimiter keeps everything in one state directory under your own user account: a configuration file, a cache, a lock, and the optional manual document. This page says where that is and what each file does.

state-directory.title: The state directory
state-directory.caption: Where the state directory lives on each platform
state-directory.permissions: The directory is created with restrictive permissions where the platform supports them. A path that turns out to be a symbolic link is rejected rather than followed.

config.role: Written by openlimiter init. Records the connector list, whether each one was detected, and the statusline layout.

cache.role: The one cache every command reads and every writer merges into.

lock.role: Held by writers only. Readers never take it.

manual.role: Optional. Quota you maintain by hand. See <docs>ingestion</docs> for the shape.

cache-behaviour.title: How the cache behaves

bullets.oneFile: One schema, one file, one lock. There are no competing state files to reconcile.
bullets.readers: Readers never take the lock. A reader opens the file, validates that open descriptor, and reads through it, so a path swapped after the check cannot redirect the bytes.
bullets.writers: Writers take the lock, and the read, the merge, and the write all happen inside it. A lock older than five seconds is treated as abandoned and reclaimed.
bullets.atomic: Every replacement flushes to stable storage before the rename, so a reader observes either the previous content or the new content and never a partial file.

cache-behaviour.doctor: Cache health is visible at any time through openlimiter doctor, which prints the cache status and how many rows were dropped for failing validation.

statusline.title: The statusline layout
statusline.intro: The statusline draws one compact cell per provider: a name, a five block bar, and the percentage, with the overall reason code and the routing recommendation leading the row. Six keys in the configuration file decide how that row is built, and openlimiter config is how they are read and changed.

statusline-keys.title: Every key
statusline-keys.caption: The statusline keys and what each one accepts

order.meaning: The order the cells appear in. Whatever you list comes first; every provider you leave out follows the built in order behind it, which is the subscription plans and then the credit and API meters. NONE is the way back to that built in order. Default NONE.

meters.meaning: A provider with several meters shows the one closest to its cap, or all of them as separate cells named PROVIDER:METER. Meters order session, daily, weekly, monthly, credits. Default worst.

width.meaning: The columns one row may spend before the line stacks. Nothing measures your terminal: a statusline host runs the command with no terminal attached, so the number here is the number honoured. Default 140.

rows.meaning: How many rows the layout may use. Default 2.

bars.meaning: False restores the single plain line from 0.1.0, byte for byte. Default true.

color.meaning: auto follows the terminal, which for a statusline host usually means no colour, because the host captures the output rather than handing the command a terminal. always is how you say the host understands escape codes. Default auto.

statusline.calloutBody: The environment variable is the one setting a person makes once for every tool on the machine, so a configuration file inside one tool does not overrule it. With NO_COLOR set, the bars are drawn in # and . and no escape code is emitted at all.

statusline-commands.title: Reading and writing them
statusline-commands.oneKey: One key at a time, validated before it is written. A value the key cannot use exits 2 and names what it wanted, and nothing partial is written, because the whole document is replaced atomically. Statusline keys are the only thing this command mutates: the connector list belongs to openlimiter init, and any other key exits 2.
statusline-commands.reinit: Re running openlimiter init keeps whatever is configured here and only redetects the connectors. A statusline key this version cannot read falls back to its default rather than stopping the draw, so a hand edited typo in one field never costs you the other five.

statusline-stacking.title: When the row runs out of room
statusline-stacking.body: The line stacks instead of truncating. A break lands between two cells and never inside one, and two rows is the ceiling. Past that the providers closest to their caps are the ones kept, and the last row ends by saying how many it could not show.

statusline-plain.title: The 0.1.0 line, on request
statusline-plain.body: The format before this layout was one plain line with no bars. If you wrote a script against it, bars false returns it exactly, and a test pins that exact string so it cannot drift.

claude-code.title: Claude Code settings
claude-code.intro: Use the absolute path to your clone. Forward slashes work on every platform, including Windows.

which-writes.title: Which of the two writes
which-writes.body: Only the statusline. It is the path that receives the session payload, so it is the path that updates the cache. The hook reads and never writes.

credentials.title: Credentials
credentials.calloutTitle: Keys belong in the operating system credential store
credentials.calloutBody: The only credential OpenLimiter has any concept of is an OpenRouter key, and it belongs in your operating system credential store. It must never appear in repository files, cache files, exports, diagnostics, fixtures, or logs. Provider authentication artifacts are opened read only and are never rewritten, backed up, repaired, or migrated.
credentials.stub: The credential library call sits behind an interface, and the adapter is stubbed in this release, so openlimiter init cannot store a key until a driver is supplied. Nothing else on your machine is touched.

detection.title: Connector detection
detection.intro: Detection is a pure function of the environment the CLI hands a connector. Facts only the CLI can observe, such as a manual document sitting in the state directory, arrive as explicit markers, which is why openlimiter doctor never claims a connector is ready when it could not receive data.
detection.corrupt: A cache that would not parse, or one that parsed with rows thrown out, adds one more line in red saying so. It reports against the cache rather than against a provider, because a corrupt file cannot be trusted to say whose reading it held.

cli.title: CLI reference
cli.metaTitle: CLI reference: commands, flags and exit codes
cli.description: Every command the CLI accepts today, with its flags, its output, and its exit codes.
cli.lead: Ten commands, one binary. Agent tools and people get the same interface, and every command reports a genuine failure rather than inventing a number.

overview.title: Overview
overview.install: Install the global command with npm install -g openlimiter, then run each example exactly as shown.

init.body: Writes local configuration to the state directory, recording every connector and whether it was detected. It reports the detected list, or none.

snapshot.intro: Prints the cached quota as a table. With --refresh it first asks every connector for meters, folds what survives validation into the cache, and then prints. Exits 3 when no bounded quota data exists.
snapshot.columns: Eight columns, always eight, separated by one space, so a script can split a row without guessing. BAR is a ten block meter, drawn in colour when the terminal supports it and in # and . when it does not or when NO_COLOR is set. AMOUNT carries the money for a plan that is priced rather than rationed. RESET is the instant the window turns over and IN is how long that is from now. A column with nothing to say reads NONE rather than disappearing.
snapshot.failures: A connector that was handed a payload and could not read it, or a reading the validator threw out, adds one line under the table in red, naming the provider and one fixed sentence. That sentence is always one of ours: no text a provider sent ever reaches your terminal.

statusline.intro: Renders the status row for a statusline host. It reads standard input first, so a Claude Code session payload is ingested and rendered in the same call, then falls back to the cache. This is the only command that writes as a side effect of being displayed.
statusline.cells: The overall reason code leads, then the routing recommendation, then one compact cell per provider: a name, a five block bar, and the percentage. Five blocks rather than the ten the table draws, because a status row is shared with a model name, a branch and a directory, and it has to read at a glance. The percentage is truncated like everywhere else, so a bar never lights a block the reading has not earned.
statusline.order: Subscription providers come first and credit or API providers last, so a window that refills on a clock is never read next to a balance that does not come back. Within a provider the meters order session, daily, weekly, monthly, credits, and the cell shows the meter closest to its cap. The full set is one openlimiter snapshot away, or set statusline.meters all to put every meter in the row as its own cell.
statusline.stacking: A row wider than its budget stacks rather than truncating. The break lands between two cells and never inside one, because half a bar reads as a reading and is not one. Two rows is the ceiling. Past that the providers closest to their caps are kept, and the last row ends by saying how many it could not show.
statusline.calloutTitle: The old line is still one setting away
statusline.calloutBody: openlimiter config set statusline.bars false returns the single plain line that 0.1.0 printed, byte for byte, for anything already parsing it. A test pins that exact string, so the escape hatch cannot rot quietly.

config.body: Reads and changes the statusline layout in the configuration file. Every key is validated before it is written, a rejected value exits 2 and names what it wanted, and nothing outside the statusline section can be changed by this command. See <docs>configuration</docs> for what each key accepts.

hook.body: Emits the agent context block from the cache. It performs no network access, writes nothing, and injects nothing when every provider is unknown. See <docs>agent context</docs> for the exact format.

ingest.body: Accepts a quota document from any script or agent, on standard input or inline with --payload. Without --provider the document is a manual document. With it, the document goes to that connector's parser and keeps that connector's labels.

doctor.body: Reports connector detection, freshness, drift, and cache health. Drift stays UNVERIFIED until an explicit verifier exists, and the output is redacted by design.

demo.body: Renders synthetic fixtures so you can see the output shape without any real account. Every value it prints is invented. The block below is the real output of that command, pasted in unedited.

export.body: Prints the cache as canonical JSON, suitable for a script to parse. Exits 3 when the cache holds no bounded quota data.

serve.body: Serves a read only snapshot of your quota on your own local network, so a phone on the same network can see it. Prints the address and a QR code to scan. A fresh token is generated every time the command starts, and it rides in the URL fragment after #t=, which a server never receives. The page moves that token into the tab's own sessionStorage and cleans the address bar on first load, so no browser history anywhere keeps the capability. Every refetch after that sends the token as an Authorization: Bearer header instead of a URL parameter. An address printed by last release, with the token as a query parameter, still answers for this one release, so nothing already scanned or saved breaks.
serve.calloutTitle: Anyone who can see the screen can read the quota
serve.calloutBody: The address and the code ARE the key: anyone who can see this screen, or a photograph of it, can read your quota for as long as the command keeps running. This listens on every interface on the machine, so do not port forward this port and do not open it on a firewall. It is meant for a trusted home or office network, never for the open internet, and it exposes only the bounded fields the agent context carries.

exit-codes.title: Exit codes
exit-codes.caption: Exit codes and what they mean

rows.usage: A usage error, such as an unknown provider id.
rows.noData: No bounded quota data is available.

exit-codes.calloutBody: Both are invoked by another tool, so they report unknown instead of breaking their host. Every other command surfaces a failure on standard error using a fixed set of strings that never carry provider text, paths taken from a payload, or secrets.

bullets.stdin: Standard input is bounded and time limited, so a command never waits on a stream that does not end.
bullets.truncated: Displayed percentages are truncated rather than rounded, so no surface can report a cap that was not reached.
bullets.flags: --provider and --payload each need a value. Passing the flag without one is a usage error.
bullets.noNetwork: In this release no command reaches the network. Every path is a parser over something already on your machine.

security.title: Security and privacy
security.description: What OpenLimiter guarantees, what it deliberately does not do, and how to report a problem.
security.lead: OpenLimiter runs on your machine and reads things that are already there. This page states what that guarantees, what it deliberately does not do, and how to report a problem.

bullets.noServer: There is no OpenLimiter server. Nothing is sent to the project authors, because there is nowhere to send it.
bullets.noTelemetry: There is no telemetry. No command sends usage, diagnostics, identifiers, prompts, or quota state anywhere.
bullets.hookNoNetwork: The hook makes no network request. It reads the local cache and nothing else.
bullets.noEgress: This release performs no egress at all. No connector contacts a provider. Every one of them is a parser over data something else already produced.
bullets.unknownNeverZero: Unknown never becomes zero. Missing, expired, malformed, and unrecognised input all resolve to unknown.
bullets.readOnlyArtifacts: Provider authentication artifacts are read only. They are never rewritten, backed up, repaired, or migrated.

injection-boundary.title: The agent context boundary
injection-boundary.intro: Provider text is untrusted data. A block injected into a prompt is an injection surface, so the pipeline is built so that no provider supplied text can reach it.

bullets.parsers: Connector parsers select known numeric fields and known timestamps. They discard labels, messages, account text, markup, and every unknown field.
bullets.advice: The advice engine emits only provider enum codes, reason enum codes, bounded percentages, freshness enum codes, and timestamps.
bullets.adapter: The Claude Code adapter validates all of those again and wraps them in an explicit untrusted data boundary before anything is written.
bullets.unknown: If every provider is unknown, the adapter injects nothing.

injection-boundary.exactBlock: The exact block, field by field, is on the <docs>agent context page</docs>.

secrets.title: Secret handling
secrets.intro: The only credential the project has a concept of is an OpenRouter key, and it belongs in your operating system credential store. It must never appear in repository files, cache files, exports, diagnostics, fixtures, or logs. The credential library call sits behind an interface, and the tests use only a memory implementation with a synthetic key.

local-state.title: Local state
local-state.body: The state directory is created with restrictive permissions where the platform supports them, a path that turns out to be a symbolic link is rejected rather than followed, and every file replacement is atomic. See <docs>configuration</docs> for the paths.

honest-limits.title: Honest limitations
honest-limits.calloutTitle: Read this before you rely on a number

bullets.noOfficialApi: Most consumer subscription providers offer no official quota API. Several connectors therefore describe unofficial interfaces that can change or disappear without notice.
bullets.unverified: Every connector ships marked UNVERIFIED. Nothing here has been confirmed against a live account by an explicit verifier.
bullets.opencode: The OpenCode connector describes an authenticated page shape and carries high automation risk. Treat it as the most fragile of the six.
bullets.adviceOnly: OpenLimiter provides routing advice. It does not route requests automatically, bypass limits, or change how your agent authenticates.

future-egress.title: If a future connector goes to the network
future-egress.intro: This release performs no provider egress. A future connector that does would have to satisfy all of the following before it could ship.

bullets.transport: Use secure transport and reject any redirect outside that host.
bullets.bounds: Set a short timeout and bound the response size.
bullets.sendNothing: Send no cache content, no other provider state, no prompts, no source code, and no diagnostics.

reporting.title: Reporting a problem
reporting.address: Report a suspected vulnerability privately to security@openlimiter.com. Include a concise description, the affected version, reproduction steps using synthetic data, and the expected impact. Do not include real credentials or provider account data. That address is a project placeholder until the public security intake is activated.
reporting.scope: In scope: secret disclosure, provider artifact mutation, unsafe cache behaviour, symbolic link bypass, parser bounds bypass, agent context injection, and unexpected network egress. Connector drift with no security impact is a compatibility issue, so please open a connector request instead. The full policy lives in <policy>SECURITY.md</policy> and the reasoning in <threat>THREAT_MODEL.md</threat>.
reporting.supported: Only the latest released version receives security fixes during the initial development period.

roadmap.title: Roadmap
roadmap.description: What is planned and not yet built: mobile applications, encrypted sync, and signed builds with an automatic update channel.
roadmap.lead: What is on this page is not yet built, with one exception noted at the top so nothing here reads as a promise about something that already ships. None of the planned work can be downloaded, bought, or waited for on a list. It is written down so the shape of the project is honest about where it is going.

not-available.title: Read this first
not-available.calloutBody: Everything called planned below does not exist today. There is no mobile application in any store and no synchronisation service running anywhere. What works today is documented on the rest of this site, and the difference between the two is deliberate.

desktop.title: Shipped: the desktop application
desktop.intro: A small desktop application with a tray icon next to the system clock, reading the same local cache the command line tool writes, so quota is glanceable without a terminal open. It is built, and packaged builds for Windows, macOS and Linux are all attached to the release on GitHub.

bullets.status: Status: shipped on Windows, macOS and Linux. Every build is on the releases page, and the download page links each file directly.
bullets.signing: Planned: code signing on Windows and notarisation on macOS. Until those are done, SmartScreen and Gatekeeper warn on first run.
bullets.updates: Planned: an automatic update channel. There is none today.

mobile.title: Planned: native mobile applications
mobile.intro: Applications for iOS and Android, so a long running window can be checked away from the desk. The web app already installs to a phone home screen and works offline, which is the part of this that exists.

bullets.status: Status: planned. Nothing is submitted to any store.
bullets.dependsOnSync: A phone cannot read a file on your laptop, so a native application that shows the numbers on your desk machine depends on the synchronisation work below.

sync.title: Planned: OpenLimiter Pro
sync.intro: Everything that can only run on a server, gathered into one planned paid tier at $5 a month, founding price. Nothing that runs locally today moves behind it: Pro sells servers and service, not switches. See <pricing>pricing</pricing> for the card as it stands.

bullets.status: Status: planned. No service exists, there is no checkout and no waiting list.
bullets.sync: Encrypted synchronisation of quota state across your own devices.
bullets.push: Push notifications to your phone when a window nears its cap.
bullets.smartLimiter: A smart limiter: quota aware routing between your models, driven by live budget state.
bullets.email: Email alerts and a weekly digest, with delivery rules for quiet hours.
